```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(hdrm)
```

## Introduction

The `hdrm` package provides tests for mean vectors in high-dimensional
repeated-measures designs. It contains two main functions: `hdrm_single()` for
the one-group setting [@Pauly2015] and `hdrm_grouped()` for designs with
multiple independent groups [@Sattler2018; @Sattler2021].

High-dimensional repeated-measures settings arise when the dimension $d$ of
the observation vectors is large relative to the available sample sizes.
Classical multivariate procedures based on an inverse sample covariance matrix
may then no longer be applicable. The procedures implemented in `hdrm` do not
require a prespecified asymptotic relation between $d$ and the sample size.
Some of the underlying frameworks also allow the number of groups to increase.

The tests are based on standardized quadratic forms and a Pearson
approximation. Multi-group analyses can be performed with heterogeneous
covariance matrices or, under the corresponding additional assumption, with a
common covariance matrix. The package also provides subsampling and compact
representations of hypothesis matrices to reduce computation time.

This vignette gives the statistical background needed to use the package and
then illustrates the main workflow with the data sets included in `hdrm`.

## Statistical background

Let

\[
\boldsymbol X_{i,j}
\sim
N_d(\boldsymbol\mu_i,\boldsymbol\Sigma_i)
\]

denote the observation vector of subject $j$ in group $i$, with $n_i$ subjects
in group $i$ and total sample size

\[
N=\sum_{i=1}^a n_i.
\]

For one group, $a=1$. In the multi-group setting, the mean vectors are stacked
as

\[
\boldsymbol\mu
=
(\boldsymbol\mu_1^\top,\ldots,\boldsymbol\mu_a^\top)^\top.
\]

The hypotheses considered in `hdrm` can be written as

\[
H_0:\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol 0,
\]

where $\boldsymbol T$ is a projection matrix. In the multi-group setting, the
package uses hypotheses of the form

\[
\boldsymbol T
=
\boldsymbol T_W\otimes\boldsymbol T_S,
\]

where $\boldsymbol T_W\in\mathbb R^{a\times a}$ describes the group structure
and $\boldsymbol T_S\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ the repeated-measurement
structure.

Writing

\[
\boldsymbol P_m
=
\boldsymbol I_m-\frac{1}{m}\boldsymbol J_m,
\]

where $\boldsymbol P_m$ denotes the $m\times m$ centering matrix, the predefined
multi-group hypotheses are:

| `hypothesis` | $\boldsymbol T_W$ | $\boldsymbol T_S$ | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `"whole"` | $\boldsymbol P_a$ | $\boldsymbol J_d/d$ | no group main effect |
| `"sub"` | $\boldsymbol J_a/a$ | $\boldsymbol P_d$ | no dimension main effect |
| `"interaction"` | $\boldsymbol P_a$ | $\boldsymbol P_d$ | no group-by-dimension interaction |
| `"identical"` | $\boldsymbol P_a$ | $\boldsymbol I_d$ | identical mean vectors |
| `"flat"` | $\boldsymbol I_a$ | $\boldsymbol P_d$ | flat profile in every group |

For one group, the only predefined hypothesis is `"flat"`,

\[
H_0:\boldsymbol P_d\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol 0.
\]

Let

\[
\overline{\boldsymbol X}
=
(\overline{\boldsymbol X}_1^\top,\ldots,
\overline{\boldsymbol X}_a^\top)^\top
\]

denote the vector obtained by stacking the group sample means. The procedures
are based on the quadratic form

\[
Q_N
=
N\overline{\boldsymbol X}^{\top}
\boldsymbol T
\overline{\boldsymbol X}.
\]

In other contexts, this quadratic form is also referred to as an ANOVA-type
statistic (ATS). For

\[
\boldsymbol\Sigma_N
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^a
\frac{N}{n_i}\boldsymbol\Sigma_i,
\]

its first two moments under the null hypothesis are

\[
E(Q_N)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\Sigma_N)
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(Q_N)
=
2\operatorname{tr}\left((\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\Sigma_N)^2\right).
\]

These quantities are used to construct the standardized statistic $W$. The
Pearson approximation additionally requires the third-order trace

\[
\operatorname{tr}\left((\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\Sigma_N)^3\right).
\]

Its parameter is

\[
f_P
=
\frac{
\operatorname{tr}^3\left((\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\Sigma_N)^2\right)
}{
\operatorname{tr}^2\left((\boldsymbol T\boldsymbol\Sigma_N)^3\right)
},
\]

and the corresponding standardized chi-squared variable is

\[
K_{f_P}
=
\frac{\chi^2_{f_P}-f_P}{\sqrt{2f_P}}.
\]

The convergence parameter

\[
\tau_P=\frac{1}{f_P}
\]

is reported by the package. Values close to zero correspond to the normal
limiting case, while values close to one correspond to the standardized
$\chi^2_1$ limiting case.

The trace estimators depend on the considered setting. With heterogeneous
covariance matrices, mixed terms such as

\[
\operatorname{tr}
(\boldsymbol T_S\boldsymbol\Sigma_i
\boldsymbol T_S\boldsymbol\Sigma_r),
\qquad i\neq r,
\]

have to be estimated. Under homogeneous covariance matrices,

\[
\boldsymbol\Sigma_1=\cdots=\boldsymbol\Sigma_a,
\]

the expressions simplify and information can be pooled across groups. This is
why `hdrm_grouped()` contains separate procedures for the two covariance
settings.

## Data input and hypothesis specification

Both main functions accept either an $N\times d$ matrix or a data frame in
long format. With matrix input, subjects are stored in rows and
repeated-measurement dimensions in columns.

Long-format input requires the columns `value`, `subject`, and `dimension`,
with one measurement per row. For `hdrm_grouped()`, the group allocation is
supplied separately through `group`. With matrix input, `group` contains one
entry per subject; with long-format input, it contains one entry per observation
row.

Regardless of the input format, the current implementation requires complete
repeated-measurement vectors. Missing values therefore have to be handled
before calling the functions. At least two repeated-measurement dimensions are
required. In addition, `hdrm_single()` requires at least three subjects,
whereas `hdrm_grouped()` requires at least two groups with at least six subjects
in each group.

Predefined hypotheses can be selected directly through `hypothesis`. Custom
hypotheses have to be supplied through matrices.

For `hdrm_single()`, a custom hypothesis is represented by one symmetric and
idempotent matrix with positive rank. For `hdrm_grouped()`, it is supplied as a
named list containing `TW` and `TS`. Both matrices have to be symmetric and
idempotent and have positive rank.

For custom hypotheses, the order of the matrices has to match the order used in
the data. In particular, the rows and columns of `TS` correspond to the
repeated-measurement dimensions, while those of `TW` correspond to the group
levels.

## One-group analysis with `hdrm_single()`

We first use the EEG data included in the package. The data originate from the
study of @EEG_dataset and are also used in the `HRM` package described by
@HRM_RJournal. The 160 subjects belong to four diagnostic groups: subjective
cognitive complaints (SCC+ and SCC-), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and
Alzheimer's disease (AD). For each subject, four EEG variables---activity,
complexity, mobility, and brain rate---are measured at ten brain locations. The
resulting observation vectors therefore have dimension $d=40$.

As a one-group example, we consider the 30 female subjects diagnosed with mild
cognitive impairment. We test whether the measurement location has an effect on
at least one of the four variables. For each variable separately, this means
testing whether its mean profile is constant across the ten locations.

The corresponding projection matrix is

\[
\boldsymbol T
=
\boldsymbol I_4\otimes\boldsymbol P_{10}.
\]

This is different from the predefined `"flat"` hypothesis, which would impose
one flat profile across all 40 dimensions. We therefore supply the projection
matrix directly.

```{r eeg-single}
data("EEG", package = "hdrm")

MCIFemale <- EEG[
  EEG$sex == "W" & EEG$group == "MCI",
]

P10 <- diag(10) - matrix(1 / 10, 10, 10)
T <- diag(4) %x% P10

res_single <- hdrm_single(
  data = MCIFemale,
  hypothesis = T
)

res_single
```

The small p-value provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis. Thus,
the measurement profile changes across locations for at least one of the four
EEG variables.

This example also shows how a custom projection matrix can be used when the
hypothesis of interest is not covered by the predefined choices.

## Multiple-group analysis with `hdrm_grouped()`

The same EEG data can also be used to illustrate the multi-group procedures in
`hdrm_grouped()`. Instead of selecting only the female MCI subjects, we now
include all female subjects and use the diagnosis as the grouping variable.
This gives four independent groups with unequal sample sizes and $d=40$
repeated-measurement dimensions.

We first test for a whole-plot effect. The corresponding null hypothesis states
that the group means, averaged over the repeated-measurement dimensions, are
equal. It is available through `hypothesis = "whole"`.

By default, `hdrm_grouped()` allows the covariance matrices to differ between
groups.

```{r eeg-grouped-heterogeneous}
EEGFemale <- EEG[EEG$sex == "W", ]

res_group_het <- hdrm_grouped(
  data = EEGFemale,
  hypothesis = "whole",
  group = EEGFemale$group,
  subsampling = FALSE,
  B = "1000*N",
  seed = 3141
)

res_group_het
```

At the usual significance levels, the whole-plot hypothesis is not rejected.

If homogeneous covariance matrices can reasonably be assumed, the corresponding
procedure is selected with `cov.equal = TRUE`:

```{r eeg-grouped-homogeneous}
res_group_hom <- hdrm_grouped(
  data = EEGFemale,
  hypothesis = "whole",
  group = EEGFemale$group,
  subsampling = FALSE,
  B = "1000*N",
  cov.equal = TRUE,
  seed = 3141
)

res_group_hom
```

The whole-plot hypothesis is again not rejected at the usual significance
levels. The two calculations rely on different covariance assumptions.
`cov.equal = TRUE` should therefore only be used when the assumption

\[
\boldsymbol\Sigma_1=\cdots=\boldsymbol\Sigma_a
\]

is appropriate for the application.

### A second example: birth rates

As a short second example, the `birthrates` data [@birthrates] illustrate
matrix input and the predefined `"interaction"` hypothesis. The data contain
annual birth rates, recorded here as total fertility rates (children per
woman), for the 16 German federal states from 1990 to 2023. After transposing
the original matrix, the federal states serve as the observational units and
the years as the repeated-measurement dimensions.

```{r birthrates-example}
data("birthrates", package = "hdrm")

birthrates_matrix <- t(as.matrix(birthrates))

group <- factor(
  c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2),
  labels = c("west", "east")
)

res_birthrates <- hdrm_grouped(
  data = birthrates_matrix,
  hypothesis = "interaction",
  group = group,
  B = "1000*N",
  seed = 3141
)

res_birthrates
```

Here, `"interaction"` tests whether the temporal birth-rate profiles differ
between the two groups. The output provides strong evidence against the null
hypothesis. The example also shows the matrix input format directly:
observational units are stored in rows, repeated-measurement dimensions in
columns, and `group` contains one entry for each row.

## Computational options

High-dimensional repeated-measures procedures can become computationally
demanding. `hdrm` provides two main ways to reduce the computational effort:
companion matrices and subsampling.

### Companion matrices

With the default `AM = TRUE`, the package internally constructs companion
matrices for the supplied hypothesis matrices. These matrices are specifically
constructed to represent the same hypothesis while preserving the value of the
test statistic. Their number of rows can be reduced to the rank of the original
hypothesis matrix [@Sattler2025]. This applies to both predefined and
user-specified hypotheses.

This can reduce the size of the quadratic-form calculations when the rank is
much smaller than the original matrix dimension. For this reason, `AM = TRUE`
can usually be kept as the default. With `AM = FALSE`, the original projection
matrices are used instead.

### Subsampling

The required trace estimators can involve large numbers of combinations of
subjects. `hdrm_grouped()` therefore provides subsampling versions of these
estimators.

With `subsampling = TRUE`, the available lower-order trace estimators are also
calculated by subsampling. The third-order trace used for the Pearson
approximation is always estimated by subsampling, independently of this option.

The base subsampling budget is controlled by `B`. The default `B = "1000*N"`
lets it increase with the total sample size $N$. Larger values reduce the
additional Monte Carlo variability but require more computation time.

For heterogeneous covariance matrices, group-specific and pairwise estimators
use $B$ draws for the corresponding group or group pair, while the joint
third-order estimator uses $aB$ draws. Under homogeneous covariance matrices,
each subsampling-based trace estimator uses a total budget of $aB$, distributed
across the groups according to the number of available index combinations.

Since subsampling introduces randomness, `seed` can be supplied for
reproducible calculations. This is relevant even when `subsampling = FALSE`,
because the third-order trace estimator is still subsampling-based. Thus,
$\widehat f_P$, $\widehat\tau_P$, and the p-value can depend on `B` and `seed`.
If `subsampling = TRUE`, the test statistic can also vary between runs.

## Output and interpretation

Both functions return an object containing the test result and additional
information about the analysis. The compact printed output focuses on the
standardized test statistic $W$, the p-value, the estimated Pearson parameter
$\widehat f_P$, the tested hypothesis, and the convergence parameter

\[
\widehat\tau_P=\frac{1}{\widehat f_P}.
\]

The reported `f` should not be interpreted as the usual degrees of freedom of a
classical ANOVA. It determines the shape of the centered and standardized
chi-squared distribution used for the Pearson approximation.

The estimated $\widehat\tau_P$ indicates where the Pearson approximation lies
between the two limiting cases described above. Intermediate values are
discussed further below.

Individual components can be accessed directly, for example:

```{r output-components}
res_group_het$statistic
res_group_het$p.value
res_group_het$f
res_group_het$tau
```

The returned objects also contain the processed data, dimensions, hypothesis
matrices, and the relevant computational settings, which can be useful for
further processing or reporting.

## Limitations and further information

The procedures implemented in `hdrm` assume multivariate normally distributed
observation vectors. This is a common assumption in multivariate
repeated-measures inference, but it should still be considered when applying
the methods to real data.

The current implementation also requires complete repeated-measurement vectors.
Missing values are not handled internally and have to be treated before calling
`hdrm_single()` or `hdrm_grouped()`.

A further theoretical point concerns the convergence parameter $\tau_P$. The
available asymptotic results cover the two limiting regimes $\tau_P\to0$ and
$\tau_P\to1$. An analogous general result for intermediate limiting values is
currently not available. However, the simulation studies for the corresponding
methods show good finite-sample behavior also in intermediate settings.
Intermediate values of $\widehat\tau_P$ therefore do not by themselves
invalidate an analysis, although results close to the chosen significance
level should be interpreted with some additional caution.

For the complete theoretical assumptions, asymptotic results, and simulation
studies, see @Pauly2015, @Sattler2018, and @Sattler2021. The construction of the
companion matrices is described in @Sattler2025.
